articles.text: Girls from across the Bay Area gathered at Witter Field on Sunday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s annual “Play Like a Girl” event, a free day of hands-on activities designed to inspire girls to get involved in sports. Now in its fourth year, the event featured 29 interactive stations where girls ages two to 28 could try sports ranging from field hockey and flag football to roller derby. Each station offered equipment, space to play, and guidance from experienced athletes and coaches. Information on local classes, camps and leagues was also available for participants interested in continuing with a sport after the event. This year’s event also included Q&A sessions and meet-andgreets with two high-profile athletes: former WNBA player Layshia Clarendon and five-time Olympic gold medalist Dana Vollmer-Grant. Sports Participation Linked to Long-Term Benefits Organizers emphasized the long-term benefits of playing sports, citing research showing that girls who participate in athletics often experience improved physical and mental health, academic achievement and career outcomes. Families enjoy playing field hockey at Play Like a Girl 2025. Photos by Sophie Hess

Religion Corner - Main The world’s most visible Christians By Pastor Jim Hopkins I have long contended that the world’s most visible Christians are the Pope and the President of the United States of America. Both have great impact on the quality of life on our planet and both, on a daily basis, are observed and evaluated by people in every continent, country, county and city on this pale blue dot that we call home. While the President of the United States does not have to be a Christian, and the U.S. Constitution prohibits religious tests for holding office, every president has, even in some nominal way, identified with Christianity. This means that, in the eyes of billions of people, she or he is a walking, talking, living and breathing representative of my faith tradition. Even though I am not a Roman Catholic, I profess to belong to the catholic (universal) church. As such the pope, like the president, is a walking, talking, living and breathing representative of my larger faith tradition. It goes without saying that I am far from enamored with the way the current president represents Christianity. I am, however, very appreciative of the way the late Pope Francis represented our faith. His expansive vision, his concern for the vulnerable, his commitment to creation care, his gentle ways were laudable. With me, many are hopeful that the next pope will share his values and commitments. Which brings me to Steph Curry. I am not suggesting that he be president or pope. I am arguing that he too is one of the world’s most visible Christians and one who represents the essential values of my faith very well. As we are in the midst of the 2025 NBA playoffs, Curry is the focus of a monumental amount of media coverage. His play is analyzed. His health is evaluated. His demeanor is scrutinized. His comments are deconstructed. His character is dissected. In every area he comes across as skilled, honest, trustworthy, humble, confident and admirable. articles.text: Editor: The following letter was sent to Piedmont School Board on May 2. Dear PUSD Board of Education members and administration, Piedmonters for Inclusive Education (PIE) is a parent-led group that works collaboratively with PUSD, other parent organizations, and the broader community to support and raise awareness for families of children with disabilities and learning differences. We want to extend our sincere appreciation for your continued dedication to supporting all students’ education and well-being. We are especially grateful for the open communication and partnership we’ve had with Jean Fagin and Ariel Dolowich this year. As part of our ongoing efforts and in alignment with PIE’s founding mission to enhance educational opportunities for students with disabilities and learning differences, we are proud to offer grants to PUSD teachers. This year, we awarded nearly $7,000 in grants to 14 teachers across all PUSD schools—from preschool to high school. The funds supported a wide range of resources, including curriculum materials, database memberships, field trips, classroom furniture, and supplies such as sensory tools and graphing calculators. We collaborated closely with Jean Fagin to make sure that the most critical needs were addressed. We are deeply grateful to the many community members whose generous support and donations made these grants possible. In addition to the teacher grants, we launched our firstever Benefit Concert, featuring a local band made up of Piedmont parents. The concert raised over $4,000, with all proceeds benefiting the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Sidekicks program. Sidekicks trains local teens to support safe, fun, and inclusive after-school classes and summer camps for neurodivergent schoolaged children. We are excited about what we’ve been able to accomplish this year and look forward to continuing our collaboration in service of inclusive education in Piedmont. With appreciation, -Betty Rojas PIE Board President For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Construction has begun on a series of pedestrian, bicycle and ADA improvements along a stretch of Grand Avenue between Fairview and Greenbank avenues, part of a broader city plan to improve roadway safety and stormwater drainage. The Grand Avenue Repavement Project, which launched April 23, will include the installation of pedestrian bulb-outs, high-visibility crosswalks, ADA-compliant curb ramps, and permanent traffic-calming islands. The project will also re-pave the roadway once infrastructure improvements are completed. Construction is expected to continue through August. City officials say the project targets multiple intersections with known safety concerns. Pedestrian enhancements will be added at Grand and Greenbank, while new bicycle infrastructure — including a turn box and a flashing beacon activated by push button — will be added at Grand and Linda. At Grand and Fairview, the city will introduce its first bioswale — a landscaped drainage feature designed to filter stormwater runoff and reduce flooding. Native, drought-tolerWorkers and heavy machinery make room for improvements on the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. ant plants such as salvia, sea lavender, coyote mint and California gray rush will be installed as part of the bioswale landscaping. The Piedmont City Council awarded the construction contract to Rapid Grading Solutions in January for $1.41 million, with a total project budget of approximately $1.56 million. Funding includes a $500,000 grant from the Alameda County Transportation Commission. The work is part of the city’s ongoing implementation of its 2021 Safer Streets Plan, which identified the Grand/Linda and Grand/Greenbank intersections as high-priority locations for safety upgrades. In recent years, similar improvements have been completed on Oakland Avenue, where bulb-outs and flashing beacons were added at the Oakland/Howard and Oakland/Sunnyside intersections in 2022, and at Oakland/ Jerome and Oakland/El Cerrito in 2024. A new grant application is pending for additional safety work on Moraga Avenue. If approved, the project would install bulb-outs, high-visibility crosswalks and flashing beacons at four intersections: Moraga with Ramona, Highland, Mesa and Red Rock Road. articles.text: When students and parents show up, their voices need to be respected (TPH) Editorial Staff (Originally published April 24 at TPHnews.com/22067) Piedmont is a public school district. That means it receives government dollars, its employees are government employees, and it answers to citizens. Like jury duty, the Miranda warning, and elections, public school districts have to do it by the books– the name of the game is protocol. That means the Board of Educations has to be open to public comment. On the way into City Hall, one can pick up a 3 x 5 card, write their name, and be afforded 150 seconds to speak their mind. Last issue, TPH encouraged its readers to take advantage of this tool. The Editorial Board agreed that civic engagement of this variety plays an utterly essential role in the democratic process. Unfortunately, the March 26 Board of Education meeting dampened our enthusiasm about due process. During the meeting, several community members used their rights to defend the elementary school band program from any cuts. An email sent out earlier that week raised alarm among PUSD musicians and catalyzed the collective action. Among the speakers were heartfelt parents, students, and teachers, expressing their concern for a beloved program they believed to be under threat. After everyone who wanted to speak had done so, members of the board took time to acknowledge the concern. It became apparent that the board and the community were operating with different sets of information. The board members expressed frustration and disappointment at what they perceived as attacks from the public. “We should not all be here in this state of distress and disarray right now, and it caused a level of drama that I find very disappointing.” “If we cannot discuss possible changes, then we cannot do anything, we cannot do our jobs. And if any potential change comes with pitchforks, then it’s going to be very difficult for us to do anything.” “A lot of this angst and frustration is for naught.” The Editorial Board found this response disheartening. The role of public elected officials is to carry out the wishes of the public. Part of that includes listening to the wishes of the public. When members of a public school district attend a public meeting and use public time in a public building to defend something that they are afraid to lose, they are not touting pitchforks. This isn’t a shocking or upsetting situation, it’s exactly what was in the job description. Complete and utter transparency at every step of the process can feel frustrating, but the district shouldn’t be run like a business. Efficacy and efficiency come second to public engagement. We ask that the members of the board respect that public outcry is part of the deal. Things will get ugly sometimes, but that’s the role the public sometimes takes. The administrators’ role is to not take it personally.

articles.text: Education As members of the Piedmont Board of Education, we want to assure our students and community stakeholders that you are being heard. We listen to every comment and we read every letter you send. We appreciate the passion and care that our community brings to Board meetings – it is a foundational strength of our community. Having been parent volunteers ourselves, we understand the desire to engage and the need to be heard. We welcome community engagement and recognize that effective governance often involves difficult conversations and decisions that not everyone will agree with. In recent months, there has been strong advocacy around several issues. We understand the frustration when people feel unheard or when a decision doesn’t go their way. However, a different outcome doesn’t mean you weren’t heard. In addition, the Board and administration sometimes work with information that isn’t public yet. In some cases, a decision hasn’t been made, and in others, sensitive topics require confidentiality. We don’t aim to withhold information. A good example of this was the March 26th Board meeting. Earlier this year, our elementary teachers told us they wanted to improve performing arts programming. In response, we asked the superintendent to move forward with the process, and a committee of elementary educators got to work discussing and ultimately proposing improvements to our elementary performing arts programming. Before their recommendations were brought to the Board, a couple of teachers – without all of the information – communicated to students and parents that a decision had been made to cut band from the elementary music program and urged them to speak out. As a result, many stakeholders showed up at the March 26th meeting upset about a staff-led decision that was still in process. Naturally, this led to confusion and frustration. As Board members, our concern that night was not with those who spoke up; it was with the fact that inaccurate information had been circulated. We are grateful to students and parents who took time to speak about the elementary music program because your voices, opinions, and experiences are all essential to our work. However, it is our hope that these exchanges take place with mutual respect and some level of trust. The community elected us to bring about a number of changes in the district – and in recent months, we have done just that. Public service is complex, and many decisions involve difficult tradeoffs. Our role is to consider all available information and make the best decision we can for the district as a whole. In the case of the elementary music program, information was not ready at the March 26th meeting, but was ready at the April 23rd meeting when the Board approved the recommendation from our teachers. It is our love of and deep respect for our community, students, schools, and public education as an institution that drove us to serve on the all volunteer PUSD School Board. It is what motivates us to show up for difficult conversations and to make hard decisions. Yet, we too are human and get frustrated. Criticism is difficult to manage when it is rooted in misinformation or miscommunication. Our objective is not to shut down dissenting voices but to engage in fruitful, productive conversations that drive us towards our shared objective: ensuring all our students continue to receive the high quality education that they deserve. In partnership, Lindsay Thomasson, Board President Ruchi Medhekar, Board Vice President Susy Struble, Board Trustee Max Roman, Board Trustee Michael Malione, Board Trustee

In some cases, a decision hasn’t been made, and in others, sensitive topics require confidentiality. We don’t aim to withhold information. A good example of this was the March 26th Board meeting. Earlier this year, our elementary teachers told us they wanted to improve performing arts programming. In response, we asked the superintendent to move forward with the process, and a committee of elementary educators got to work discussing and ultimately proposing improvements to our elementary performing arts programming. Before their recommendations were brought to the Board, a couple of teachers – without all of the information – communicated to students and parents that a decision had been made to cut band from the elementary music program and urged them to speak out. As a result, many stakeholders showed up at the March 26th meeting upset about a staff-led decision that was still in process. Naturally, this led to confusion and frustration. As Board members, our concern that night was not with those who spoke up; it was with the fact that inaccurate information had been circulated. We are grateful to students and parents who took time to speak about the elementary music program because your voices, opinions, and experiences are all essential to our work. However, it is our hope that these exchanges take place with mutual respect and some level of trust. The community elected us to bring about a number of changes in the district – and in recent months, we have done just that. Public service is complex, and many decisions involve difficult tradeoffs. Our role is to consider all available information and make the best decision we can for the district as a whole. In the case of the elementary music program, information was not ready at the March 26th meeting, but was ready at the April 23rd meeting when the Board approved the recommendation from our teachers. It is our love of and deep respect for our community, students, schools, and public education as an institution that drove us to serve on the all volunteer PUSD School Board. It is what motivates us to show up for difficult conversations and to make hard decisions. Yet, we too are human and get frustrated. Criticism is difficult to manage when it is rooted in misinformation or miscommunication. Our objective is not to shut down dissenting voices but to engage in fruitful, productive conversations that drive us towards our shared objective: ensuring all our students continue to receive the high quality education that they deserve. articles.text: How parents can make it count When Maya, 22, was asked to name her clearest childhood memory, she skipped the homework, the carpools and even her tenth-birthday cake. “It’s the night we slept in the backyard to watch a meteor shower,” she said. While those “Mountain Memories” were momentous in mind and heart, the “Valleys” make up most memories – both are valuable to “unblur” their childhood. What the study covered Over 20 years, I conducted 2+ hour conversations with more than 1,000 adults aged 19-30 from over 30 countries (25 percent international; mixed socioeconomic backgrounds). They answered dozens of open-ended prompts ranging from “What rituals were meaningful to you?” to “List your ten most salient memories from ages 8-18.” The result is a map of childhood recollection that parents can turn into an action plan. The mountains Planned and unplanned milestones. First concerts, graduation road-trips, a spontaneous camping night in a thunderstorm, as well as births, deaths and other life-course jolts, dominate narrative space. These episodic spikes are remembered in cinematic detail decades later—especially when photographs or keepsakes exist to cue retrieval, a phenomenon long supported by memory research. The valleys Small rituals with big footprints. Weekly pancake breakfasts, Friday-night board-game marathons, and bedtime readalouds form the gentle terrain in-between. Interviewees recalled the fact that these rituals simply happened, far more than they recalled what was said during them—evidence that predictability, not polish, drives emotional resonance. Developmental psychologists have repeatedly linked family rituals to greater well-being and resilience in youth. The surprising blanks Overarchingly, adults remembered far less of their childhood than you might imagine; after the “big events,” the rest of upper grade school onward was summarized by them in under 30 minutes! Childhood is largely a blur before age seven. Most respondents remembered very few specific memories before third grade, a pattern that matches “childhood amnesia” findings in cognitive science. But that isn’t always or necessarily true . . . keep reading. Group activities such as sports seasons were also stored in “collapsed” form—people remembered the vibe, not the playby-play, unless a single pivotal moment (the championship goal) broke through. Action plan: where attention beats perfection The data suggest two leverage points: anchor the calendar with a handful of big, well-documented adventures, and weave in a dozen-plus micro-rituals that happen with metronomic reliability. Below is menu parents can mix and match – take some picks, AND create your own. How to use the table: 1. Pick at least one ritual from each row to cover multiple memory “channels” (sensory, spatial, narrative, values-based). 2. Lock them onto the calendar—consistency, more than elaborateness, is what etches them into long-term memory. 3. Add lightweight documentation (a single photo, a 30-second voice memo) to give future adults the cues that science shows can unlock richer childhood stories. For the mountain moments – vacations, graduations, first concerts – lean into spectacle and documentation: stage a quirky group photo, record a short reflection video on the spot, and print a few images for the fridge. Photos are not vanity; they become the retrieval keys that unlock richer narratives later in life. The takeaway of simple rituals and treating the occasional milestone like the festival it is, parents trade ephemeral logistics for memories that outlast childhood’s inevitable blur. In a word, it is attention not extravagance that etches family into story. Randall Grayson P.h.D (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about summer program, family camps, and twoweek sessions can be found at www.campaugusta.org. Food & Kitchen Bonding Sunday pancake bar Gratitude jar at dinner One‑song kitchen dance‑off Turns a daily necessity into a multisensory micro‑celebration. Repetition builds scent‑ and music‑linked memory cues with almost zero extra cost. Outdoor & Nature Adventures Solstice sunrise hike First‑snow cocoa walk Neighborhood night hike Annual photo‑scavenger hunt Novel landscapes plus mild exertion elevate adrenaline and dopamine, deepening autobiographical encoding; seasonal anchors give the brain temporal hooks. Milestones & Memory‑ Making Birthday interview video New‑school‑year time capsulea Hand‑written postcards on trips Flags major transitions and collects physical artifacts that function as potent retrieval cues decades later. Growth & Connection Rituals Monthly “yes day” Quarterly volunteer day “Big fail” celebration night Cousins’ trivia showdown Builds agency, empathy, and shared mastery; normalizes failure as a bonding experience and spotlights family values in action. Creative Expression & Storytelling Seasonal story circle by firelight Home talent showcase evening Shared creation yields highly specific, emotion‑laden memories; artistic products become tangible mnemonic anchors. Mind‑Body Well‑Being Rituals Couples predictable bodily movement with reflective practice, reinforcing awareness—shown to enhance mood regulation and memory consolidation.

articles.text: In 2023 Piedmont Fire Department celebrated winning three awards at the Big Climb in Oracle Park, a fundraiser for the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society. The four-man team earned fastest team, fastest individual, and top fundraising team. Pictured are Nicholas Christ (left), Brian Protheroe, Capt. Justin McNulty, and Anthony Renteria. Piedmont Fire Department will participate in the Big Climb on Saturday, May 10, a race traversing through the upper deck of San Francisco’s Oracle Park as a fundraiser for the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society (LLS). The department’s third year of participation in the event means more this year as one of its own members, Engineer Russ San Filippo, was diagnosed with leukemia in December. Captain Justin McNulty and the department have so far raised $5,895 and need some additional support to reach their $10,000 fundraising goal. Participating this year are Capt. McNulty, Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, Brian Protheroe, Lucas Romero, and Nadder Shehadeh. In their first two years of participation, 2023 and 2024, PFD won all three categories of competition. McNulty is the twotime fastest individual, and the team has won two years in a row as the fastest team and top first responder fundraising team. Piedmont’s firefighters have added extra training to their ordinary workout regiments by running the bleachers at Witter Field. The grueling Big Climb race goes up and down each of the 28 sections in Giants stadium’s steep upper deck. “You’re burning, your lungs are on fire, but that’s nothing compared to what these people had to go through, and their battles and tribulations. So it’s a good motivator,” explained McNulty. The Big Climb takes place in 13 cities across the country annually in iconic locations including Citi Field in New York and Philadelphia’s Subaru Park. Last year’s event occurred during an unusual springtime San Francisco downpour. Despite the elements, over 3,000 climbers participated to support LLS. LLS has invested over $1.8 billion since 1949 towards fighting and curing leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma, and other blood cancers. Overall, the 5-year relative survival rate for leukemia has more than doubled from 34% (1975-1977) to 70% (2013-2019). Donate to the Piedmont Fire Department’s Big Climb page at https://pages.lls.org/bigclimb/ gba/bigclimbsf 25/PiedmontFireDepartment. In 2023 Piedmont Fire Department celebrated winning three awards at the Big Climb in Oracle Park, a fundraiser for the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society. The four-man team earned fastest team, fastest individual, and top fundraising team. Pictured are Nicholas Christ (left), Brian Protheroe, Capt. Justin McNulty, and Anthony Renteria. By Jay Russell Piedmont Fire Department will participate in the Big Climb on Saturday, May 10, a race traversing through the upper deck of San Francisco’s Oracle Park as a fundraiser for the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society (LLS). The department’s third year of participation in the event means more this year as one of its own members, Engineer Russ San Filippo, was diagnosed with leukemia in December. Captain Justin McNulty and the department have so far raised $5,895 and need some additional support to reach their $10,000 fundraising goal. Participating this year are Capt. McNulty, Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, Brian Protheroe, Lucas Romero, and Nadder Shehadeh. In their first two years of participation, 2023 and 2024, PFD won all three categories of competition. McNulty is the twotime fastest individual, and the team has won two years in a row as the fastest team and top first responder fundraising team. Piedmont’s firefighters have added extra training to their ordinary workout regiments by running the bleachers at Witter Field. The grueling Big Climb race goes up and down each of the 28 sections in Giants stadium’s steep upper deck. “You’re burning, your lungs are on fire, but that’s nothing compared to what these people had to go through, and their battles and tribulations. So it’s a good motivator,” explained McNulty. The Big Climb takes place in 13 cities across the country annually in iconic locations including Citi Field in New York and Philadelphia’s Subaru Park. Last year’s event occurred during an unusual springtime San Francisco downpour. Despite the elements, over 3,000 climbers participated to support LLS. LLS has invested over $1.8 billion since 1949 towards fighting and curing leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma, and other blood cancers. Overall, the 5-year relative survival rate for leukemia has more than doubled from 34% (1975-1977) to 70% (2013-2019). articles.text: Assalian - Davis win doubles consolation bracket Staff Photos Lucas Smolko with coach Jim Landes (left) and assistant coach Corey Reich after winning the league championship and being named the League Player of the Year. Piedmont High tennis player Lucas Smolko, a junior, got the job done, winning his second consecutive Western Alameda County Conference singles title in the league individual tournament on Saturday, May 3 at Chabot College in Hayward. He becomes the first athlete at PHS, boys or girls, to win back-to-back WACC titles since the league’s inception in 2012. In the championship match, Smol ko defeated Bishop O’Dowd’s Neo Chai in three sets, dominating the first and third sets toward a 6-1, 4-6, 6-2 win. It was a windy day at Chabot, especially in the second and third sets. “I was playing well in the first set, there was very little wind and I was moving my feet. Then the wind picked up in the second set and I stopped moving my feet as well and started missing forehands I was hitting in the first set. In the third set I just adjusted my movement and tried to get more top spin,” Smolko said. Smolko was the top seed in the tournament and also won the WACC Player of the Year award. He defeated O’Dowd’s Ollie Pakzad in the first , 6-1, 6-3, won 6-1, 6-2 over Castro Valley’s Advaith Sathyan in the quarterfinals, and then beat Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar, 6-3, 6-0 in the semifinals. His title win against Chai was a rematch of last year’s WACC singles finals. The two also faced one another twice in this year’s regular season, both of which Smolko won. “We know each other pretty well. It’s definitely a different dynamic than playing someone I have no experience against,” Smolko said. Smolko is set to play in this year’s Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament at Vintage High School in Napa on Friday and Saturday, May 9-10. He reached the semifinals in last year’s singles bracket. The freshman duo of Joey Assalian and Ben Davis put on a strong display in winning the consolation doubles. After falling 6-1, 6-0 in the first round to No. 4 seed Marcello Sacnelari and Olive Liao, the pair defeated Castro Valley’s Elijah Song and Dylan Kwan 8-3 and then defeated teammates from Piedmont Hunter Fasteau and Luca LaForte 8-6 in the consolation semifinals. In the consolation finals, the pair beat Alameda’s Kyle Banducci and Keenan Chan in straight sets 6-4, 6-3 after falling behind early in the first set. “Throughout the tournament, we played a lot of good opponents. We realized we just have to be aggressive. I think our teamwork in that regard definitely improved,” Assalian said “We realized we were over-hitting and missing volleys. We started approaching more, hitting it a little lighter and just being more consistent,” Davis said. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont fell to the Dragons in the WACC Tournament semifinals, and now look ahead to the North Coast Section playoffs. The Highlanders’ boys’ lacrosse team was eliminated from the Western Alameda County Conference tournament in the semifinals, falling 11-5 to rival Bishop O’Dowd at Witter Field on Wednesday, April 30. PHS beat the Dragons 8-7 during the regular season on April 4. “We needed to find the opportunity to show who we really are and tonight wasn’t it. O’Dowd played a really good game and deserved to win,” said first-year Piedmont coach Paul Pappas. Piedmont started well, ending the first quarter in a 2-2 deadlock. But as turnovers began piling up O’Dowd piled on shots. The Highlanders committed 17 turnovers on the night. “We had a good week of practice, but any time you’re in playoffs, the nerves are going to be a bit different. When you have a young team, things can change,” Pappas said. The hope is the younger leaders on the roster, like junior Ian Nguyen and Timmy Kalamas, along with sophomore Connor Fredericks, will learn from the year’s struggles. “It’s just trying to get them comfortable and confident. Guys are just paying their dues and getting better, that’s all we can ask for. These losses hurt, but we’re getting better,” Pappas said. Connor Fredericks scored two goals against Bishop O’Dowd. PHS received the No. 13 seed in the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs and faced No. 4 Foothill yesterday, Tuesday, May 6. Brayer found Connor Fredericks for a goal. articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), the oldest youth orchestra in California, will feature two of its top student musicians in a spring concert on Saturday, May 17, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The concert is part of YPSO’s 88th season and marks the 36th year under music director David Ramadanoff, a veteran Bay Area conductor and educator. Ramadanoff, a former assistant conductor of the San Francisco Symphony under Seiji Ozawa, has led YPSO since the late 1980s. The orchestra includes 80 musicians between the ages of 11 and 18, representing a wide stretch of the Bay Area from Napa to Fremont. This spring’s program features classical works from Mozart to Rachmaninoff, as well as solo performances by violinist Carolyn Ren and cellist Donghu Kim—two winners of the orchestra’s annual Concerto Competition. Ren, 16, will perform the third movement of Wieniawski’s Violin Concerto No. 2, a Romantic-era piece with sweeping melodies and brisk technical runs. “It’s such an exciting concerto, especially with all the fast spiccato and playful energy,” she said. Kim, 17, will take on Tchaikovsky’s Variations on a Rococo Theme, a nod to the Classical style of Mozart that emphasizes subtlety and ornamentation over sheer virtuosity. “It’s about finding the right color and phrasing in every variation,” he said. The program will open with Mozart’s Magic Flute Overture and close with Rachmaninoff’s Symphonic Dances, the Russian composer’s final orchestral work. In addition to the concert, YPSO will launch its annual online auction fundraiser on May 17. The auction, which runs through the end of the month, aims to raise $10,000 to support scholarships, outreach programs and operating costs. Items up for bid include gift certificates, musical instruments, and experiences with Bay Area artists and venues. Parents say the program offers more than music education. “YPSO has given my daughter not just the chance to play amazing music, but also to be part of something larger than herself,” said Christina Lee, a parent from Oakland. “It’s rare to find a program that challenges kids musically while also teaching them leadership and collaboration.” An open rehearsal is scheduled for Friday, May 16, from 6 to 9 p.m., offering prospective students and families a behindthe-scenes look at the final preparations. Admission is free, and student tickets to the concert are available at no charge with a valid student ID. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO was the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. The idea came from local harpist Clarabelle Bell, who was inspired by a youth orchestra in Portland, and realized by violinist and conductor Jessica Marcelli. More information and ticket reservations are available at ypsomusic.org/events. The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra.
articles.title: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra holds 88th Spring Concert on May 17

articles.text: Photo by Kevin Berne Asia Jackson, David Moore and Anna Sharpe in Aurora Theatre Company’s Crumbs from the Table of Joy Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Lynn Nottage’s acclaimed Crumbs from the Table of Joy is playing on the Aurora Theatre stage in Berkeley now through May 25, with post-show discussions held May 14 and 22. Directed by Elizabeth Carter, Nottage’s play follows the Crump family as they relocate from Pensacola, Florida, to Brooklyn following the death of the family matriarch. The play is told through the eyes of 17-year-old Ernestine Crump and focuses on the arrival of communist-leaning Aunt Lily, who challenges the family’s dynamics and beliefs. The play navigates the complexities of race, religion, and societal expectations during the 1950’s. When the play was first presented Off-Broadway at the Second Stage Theatre in 1995, Nottage said she chose the 1950’s because it was a time of significant social change. “Everything I had seen was in black and white,” she said at the time. “And I wanted to make it colorful. So I started writing Crumbs from the Table of Joy to try to understand that era.” Nottage is the first woman in history to win two Pulitzer Prizes for Drama, and her plays, including Crumbs from the Table of Joy, have been produced widely in the United States and throughout the world. Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello called Nottage “one of the most significant American playwrights working today,” “We’re honored to bring this early work of hers, showcasing all her insight and passion, to the Aurora stage. And I’m thrilled to welcome back director Elizabeth Carter,” Costello said. The Aurora Theatre production features Jamella Cross as Ernestine Crump, Asia Jackson as Lily Ann Green, David Moore as Godfrey Crump and Carrie Paff as Gerte Shulte. Two performances per week, Wednesday evenings and Sunday matinees, are mandatory mask-required performances. For all other performances, masks will be encouraged but not required. Visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/crumbs to purchase tickets and view showtimes.

articles.text: The smash-hit musical biopic A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical comes to San Francisco’s Golden Gate Theatre for a limited engagement from Tuesday, June 3, through Sunday, June 22. Created in collaboration with Diamond himself, the musical tells the true story of a kid from Brooklyn whose meteoric rise led him to become an American rock icon. “Some of my most thrilling nights have been while I was on tour, bringing my music to audiences across the world,” said Diamond. “Having A Beautiful Photo by Jeremy Daniel Nick Fradiani as ‘Neil - Then’ (center) and ‘The Noise’ in A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical Noise go on tour is an honor, and I can’t wait for audiences across North America to experience this show. I hope they enjoy it as much as I have.” Featuring classics like “America,” “Forever in Blue Jeans” and “Sweet Caroline,” the show stars Nick Fradiani—winner of American Idol in 2015—who went on to release his debut album Hurricane in 2016, including the hit single “Beautiful Life.” Fradiani is joined by a cast that includes Tony nominee Robert Westenberg (Neil Diamond – Now), Hannah Jewel Kohn (Marcia Murphey), Lisa Reneé Pitts (Doctor), Michael Accardo (Bert Berns/Kieve Diamond), Tuck Milligan (Fred Weintraub/Tommy O’Rourke), Kate A. Mulligan (Ellie Greenwich/Rose Diamond), and Tiffany Tatreau (Jaye Posner). The Neil Diamond Musical is produced by Ken Davenport and Bob Gaudio. “I couldn’t imagine a more perfect way to honor [Diamond’s] legacy than having A Beautiful Noise touring North America, visiting the same cities where he gave so many people so much joy,” said Davenport. Directed by Elizabeth Carter, Nottage’s play follows the Crump family as they relocate from Pensacola, Florida, to Brooklyn following the death of the family matriarch. The play is told through the eyes of 17-year-old Ernestine Crump and focuses on the arrival of communist-leaning Aunt Lily, who challenges the family’s dynamics and beliefs. The play navigates the complexities of race, religion, and societal expectations during the 1950’s. When the play was first presented Off-Broadway at the Second Stage Theatre in 1995, Nottage said she chose the 1950’s because it was a time of significant social change. “Everything I had seen was in black and white,” she said at the time. “And I wanted to make it colorful. So I started writing Crumbs from the Table of Joy to try to understand that era.” Nottage is the first woman in history to win two Pulitzer Prizes for Drama, and her plays, including Crumbs from the Table of Joy, have been produced widely in the United States and throughout the world. Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello called Nottage “one of the most significant American playwrights working today,” “We’re honored to bring this early work of hers, showcasing all her insight and passion, to the Aurora stage. And I’m thrilled to welcome back director Elizabeth Carter,” Costello said. The Aurora Theatre production features Jamella Cross as Ernestine Crump, Asia Jackson as Lily Ann Green, David Moore as Godfrey Crump and Carrie Paff as Gerte Shulte. Two performances per week, Wednesday evenings and Sunday matinees, are mandatory mask-required performances. For all other performances, masks will be encouraged but not required. Young People’s Symphony Orchestra holds 88th Spring Concert on May 17 By Tony Simons The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), the oldest youth orchestra in California, will feature two of its top student musicians in a spring concert on Saturday, May 17, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The concert is part of YPSO’s 88th season and marks the 36th year under music director David Ramadanoff, a veteran Bay Area conductor and educator. Ramadanoff, a former assistant conductor of the San Francisco Symphony under Seiji Ozawa, has led YPSO since the late 1980s. The orchestra includes 80 musicians between the ages of 11 and 18, representing a wide stretch of the Bay Area from Napa to Fremont. This spring’s program features classical works from Mozart to Rachmaninoff, as well as solo performances by violinist Carolyn Ren and cellist Donghu Kim—two winners of the orchestra’s annual Concerto Competition. Ren, 16, will perform the third movement of Wieniawski’s Violin Concerto No. 2, a Romantic-era piece with sweeping melodies and brisk technical runs. “It’s such an exciting concerto, especially with all the fast spiccato and playful energy,” she said. Kim, 17, will take on Tchaikovsky’s Variations on a Rococo Theme, a nod to the Classical style of Mozart that emphasizes subtlety and ornamentation over sheer virtuosity. “It’s about finding the right color and phrasing in every variation,” he said. The program will open with Mozart’s Magic Flute Overture and close with Rachmaninoff’s Symphonic Dances, the Russian composer’s final orchestral work. In addition to the concert, YPSO will launch its annual online auction fundraiser on May 17. The auction, which runs through the end of the month, aims to raise $10,000 to support scholarships, outreach programs and operating costs. Items up for bid include gift certificates, musical instruments, and experiences with Bay Area artists and venues. Parents say the program offers more than music education. “YPSO has given my daughter not just the chance to play amazing music, but also to be part of something larger than herself,” said Christina Lee, a parent from Oakland. “It’s rare to find a program that challenges kids musically while also teaching them leadership and collaboration.” An open rehearsal is scheduled for Friday, May 16, from 6 to 9 p.m., offering prospective students and families a behindthe-scenes look at the final preparations. Admission is free, and student tickets to the concert are available at no charge with a valid student ID. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO was the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. The idea came from local harpist Clarabelle Bell, who was inspired by a youth orchestra in Portland, and realized by violinist and conductor Jessica Marcelli. articles.text: Festival Opera board members at the Spring Soirée: Timothy Evans (left), Nina Bancroft Dickerson, Claudia Terry, Megan Dey-Toth, Jennifer Kwock-Lau, Zachary Gordin, Dr. Vivian Wing, Susie Hanson, and Keegan Dwyer Piedmont Center for the Arts hosted Festival Opera’s Spring Soirée on Saturday, May 3 at 4:00 p.m. for an evening of music and celebration inspired by the legendary Parisian musical salons. Founded in 1991, Festival Opera is a Bay-Area based opera company with the mission to advance the operatic art form and to build community by producing culturally rich and diverse programming to enlighten, educate, and entertain at the highest artistic standard. Past leadership includes the artistic direction tenures of famed soprano Olivia Stapp, Maestro Michael Morgan of the Oakland Symphony, and is currently led by baritone, conductor and impresario Zachary Gordin. Festival Opera first began performing at PCA in 2020, producing recitals and other events that were scaled to fit the venue’s intimate chambers. Now, Festival Opera presents a series of salonstyle concerts at PCA each season, encouraging the community to attend performances and meet the artists at receptions after each event at the venue. “It really is the perfect size and space to experience this special type of performance, where the audience can be close to the musicians and get involved with the music and text in a very intimate way,” said Gordin. Attendees of the Spring Soirée enjoyed the company of fellow opera lovers, patrons and artists while sipping wine, sampling sweet and savory treats from Siren Sisters Kitchen, and enjoying a live performance. articles.text: Nosy neighbors. They can be a pain—but what if one of them witnesses murder right on your block? That’s the question famed movie director Alfred Hitchcock explores in his classic thriller, Rear Window. And what if his nosy hero is played by James Stewart? And what if his girlfriend is played by Grace Kelly? And what if the murderer discovers he’s been discovered? It’s all right up there on the screen — how can an audience resist? One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Flix Fest’s next showing is indeed Rear Window, based on an ingenious Cornell Woolrich short story. Released in 1954, it centers on a recuperating news photographer, L.B. Jeffries (Stewart), who gradually comes to believe he’s witnessed a crime. Confined to a wheelchair after an accident that’s put one of his legs in a cast, he fights boredom by staring out his rear window, secretly peering with a telephoto lens and binoculars into neighboring apartments. He becomes fascinated by odd goings-on in one in particular—why is Lars Thorwald’s wife suddenly gone missing? Is the burly Thorwald mailing parts of her out of town by UPS? Assisted by girlfriend, Lisa Fremont (Kelly) and a friendly cop (Wendell Corey), Jeffries doggedly investigates, putting both himself and Lisa in peril. Hitchcock directs all this deftly, helped by a cast that includes wry and irresistible Thelma Ritter as his nurse, and Raymond Burr, who would go on to play Perry Mason and Ironside on TV, as Thorwald. Rear Window will be screened on Thursday, May 8th, at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration is encouraged and can be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is the Marilyn Monroe classic, The Seven Year Itch, to be screened on June 12th. articles.text: Shakespeare’s great comedy The Merry Wives of Windsor begat Verdi’s final opera “Falstaff”. It was an incredible formula for success. Both the play and the opera are unique. Opera Modesto featured Verdi’s opera Falstaff for its final production this season. It was a pleasure to attend and was worth a trip to Modesto. Verdi was renowned for his operatic tragedies. He admired the works of Shakespeare and drew on that great English author for his inspiration. At the age of 80 the great Italian composer decided to retire. That didn’t sit well with his admirers. They enticed him to write one more opera. “Let your final work be a comedy. We know that you love Shakespeare. Set Falstaff to music. You can conclude the opera by saying, ‘He who laughs last laughs best.’” Verdi thought this was a great idea and got to work immediately. Falstaff is a mass of contradictions. His character is a big, fat blowhard. A highly placed phony, also. The curious thing is that he is highly successful… at failure. Throughout the opera, there is considerable wordplay with puns, misdeeds, and misleads. The sum of these contradictions becomes a comedic masterpiece. The play by Shakespeare is glorious and so is the opera by Verdi. The opera was an instant success of sorts; and then a failure of sorts. Famous orchestra conductor Toscanini reintroduced it, and it has been a success ever since. In the production by Opera Modesto, the audience was treated to a superb performance. Their theater is beautiful and so was the staging and the entire performance. The orchestra was both efficient and inspired and the performers were absolutely first class. Curtain calls at the end of the opera Falstaff by Verdi in a production by Opera Modesto. The performance was beautiful from beginning to end.

Confined to a wheelchair after an accident that’s put one of his legs in a cast, he fights boredom by staring out his rear window, secretly peering with a telephoto lens and binoculars into neighboring apartments. Hitchcock directs all this deftly, helped by a cast that includes wry and irresistible Thelma Ritter as his nurse, and Raymond Burr, who would go on to play Perry Mason and Ironside on TV, as Thorwald. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, May 7, 2025 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Café Society a nugget by Woody Allen By Chris Honoré Woody Allen has made 46 films, some iconic. My initial assumptions about Café Society were that while it would be mildly entertaining, with moments that would bring about a smile, it wouldn’t be, say, Midnight in Paris. Certainly not Annie Hall or Manhattan. As it turned out, and I understand that any reaction to a film is ultimately subjective and will touch individual moviegoers in very personal ways (good and bad), Café Society was, at least for me, a wonderful surprise. Of course, some might walk away from this film and observe that it is Woody-lite. But I would disagree. Set in the 1930s, during the Great Depression, the film is steeped in Hollywood’s golden era. It’s a palm tree, boulevard-lights postcard that says, “Wish you were here.” Café Society is gorgeous to behold: the period dress, the décor, its tones and ubiquitous golden glow captivating, the interior shots of Hollywood studios so very stylish and elegant, opulent Spanish tiled mansions, breathtakingly long town cars polished to mirror shines, all of it with an overlay of sepia color, shot by the gifted cinematographer, Vittorio Storaro. The film is Woody’s homage to Hollywood during a period that lends itself to being romanticized and certainly idealized. Add Gershwin 78 rpm vinyl songs and Kristen Stewart and Jesse Eisenberg in Café Society you’re there. So completely there. While Café Society has been billed as a comedy. This is, after all, Woody Allen, master of the incisive one-liner, dialogue perfectly crafted while he agonizes about imagined maladies. But in reality it is, a love story between a young and naïve transplanted New Yorker, Bobby Dorman (Jesse Eisenberg), who ventures west to California to start a new life and hopefully find work with his uncle, s successful Hollywood agent, Phil Stern (Steve Carrell). It’s in Stern’s office that he meets Vonnie (Kristen Stewart), a young beauty who came west to act but found getting inside the industry tent all but impossible. For Bobby, it’s love at first glance. She’s stunning, innocent yet streetwise, as well as generous. And so, as Bobby struggles to find his west coast sea legs, supported by Phil and his circle of contacts, a triangle is offered up in a surprising reveal. Meanwhile uncle Ben (Cory Stoll) is intent on getting into the nightclub business and burying those who stand in his way in cement coffins at construction sites. Actually, Ben is a good guy, endearing in a kind of remorseless, gangster kind of way. In one of Woody’s great lines in the film, spoken, I believe, in voice over by Woody himself, he quotes and then embellishes Socrates, commenting that “The unexamined life is not worth living. But the examined life is no bargain.” Somehow that sentiment is perfect as Bobby struggles to find love and his place in New York, Hollywood, and once again back in New York. What is so appealing about this movie is that while there is an unspoken melancholy that frames the story, what is missing in Woody’s manic insecurities; instead, he (in the persona of Bobby) is gently reflective. The tale is familiar, yet it is told in a fresh and appealing way, underscoring that when it comes to matters of the heart, the heart trumps intellect, for better or worse. Woody also returns to his familiar and signature theme: regret. And he reiterates that from that emotion is evinced a resulting sadness, constructed of memories, that though they may fade, there still remain those unexpected moments when a time or a decision or a person now long gone will cause us to stop and gaze off into the distance and contemplate what might have been. This very brief interlude is compounded by the realization that life moves us on, inextricably, and that what once was can never be again, no matter how deeply we wish it were otherwise. And it is that sense of lingering sadness, a realization dearly purchased, that threads it way through Café Society and makes so much of this film sublime. Café Society. Meanwhile, Arrietty and her father go on a mission above the floorboards to borrow a cube of sugar, an adventure to be sure for she is fascinated by the sheer size of the bean world, something she views in all its gigantic splendor and potential danger. articles.text: Britt Robertson and Asa Butterfield in The Space Between Us Let’s be honest, the tween/teen crowd is exactly the demographic for which The Space Between Us It is a tender teenage love story that finds its sweet spot. The premise is that Gardner (Asa Butterfield) is, unexpectedly, born on Mars. His mother, an astronaut, dies giving birth. Hence, he grows up on Mars in a very controlled and insulated environment. Fast forward 16 years and Gardner is feeling very much like an adolescent, acting out with a million dollar Mars rover and insisting to his coach (and the folks that matter) that he wants above all to go to earth, a place he’s only been told about. What the adults don’t know is that he has been emailing a young girl, Tulsa (Britt Robertson), sharing feelings and images on their computers (I know, Mars to earth and back, well, it’s a stretch). Their attraction has grown. So Gardner not only wants to see earth, he wants to see Tulsa. And he wants to search for his dad, who he has never met. And thus begins his journey. He finds Tulsa, and she joins him in his search for his dad, which morphs into quite a tender adventure. Meanwhile, an unhappy NASA crowd is in the hunt for Gardner; they’re not pleased with him being out and about on his own. What he doesn’t know is that earth is not only strange and vastly different from Mars, but is also a possible threat to his health. His caretakers want desperately to find him and get him back into a controlled gravity environment. I’d judge that The Space Between Us will have the tweens and teens in its pocket from the start, all the way to the money shot at the end. There’s great music, and a nice love story, with lots of good acting on the part of Robertson and Butterfield, who have youthful chemistry. The Space Between Us. Directed by Peter Chelsom. articles.text: Lisa Anne Gaston, a wonderful wife, mother, grandmother, teacher and friend passed peacefully on April 3, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia, surrounded by her family and a few of her closest Born on an Air Force Base in Biloxi, Mississippi, and having lived in Atlanta for the past 36 years, Lisa Anne was known for her southern charm but was a true (and emphatic) California girl at heart. She spent her childhood in Piedmont, California, where she graduated from Piedmont High School in 1975. The only child of two pioneering physicians – Dr. Harper Gaston, a dedicated cardiologist, who founded the Kaiser Permanente Southeast Medical Group, and Dr. Anne Gaston, one of the very first female, board-certified neonatologists – Lisa Anne was raised with wit, determination and a passion for learning. She pursued her undergraduate studies at Bryn Mawr College, where she majored in political science. Her years at Bryn Mawr were some of her most treasured. She cherished the century-old traditions and made lifelong friends, many of whom she remained in touch with all of Never one to shy away from a challenge, she then moved to Washington D.C., earning both a Master’s Degree in Foreign Service and International Development, as well as a Juris Doctor in International Law and Legal Studies at Georgetown Lisa Anne’s professional journey was as diverse as it was impressive. She began her career practicing law in New York, California and Georgia. Once in Atlanta, she transitioned into television, where she became Vice President of Public Affairs at Turner Broadcasting. Her work creating “Interact Atlanta” earned her multiple Emmy Awards and paved the way for her eventual move to Georgia Public Broadcasting, where she was recognized as one of the “Women Making a Mark” by Atlanta Magazine. It was during her broadcasting years that she Former Piedmont resident Lisa Anne Gaston died on April 3, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. met her great love and husband of 25 years, Michael Reff. In the next chapter of her life, Lisa Anne discovered her truest calling: teaching. Earning yet another Masters Degree in Education from Agnes Scott College, she spent nine cherished years teaching English and Literature at Central Gwinnett High School. With a deep love for books and a passion for writing, she inspired her students to find confidence in their writing and empowered them to discover their own voice. She loved her students, and they loved her in return. In her final days, she received an outpouring of love and gratitude from many of her past students who shared the many ways in which Lisa Anne influenced and changed the course of their lives. Lisa Anne’s life was filled with adventure and travel with her husband, Michael, and her two daughters, Allison and Hayley Harper. She was known for her radiant smile, sharp intellect, and gift for finding joy and beauty in the everyday. She never hesitated to speak her mind, stood strong in her convictions, and moved through life with an unwavering sense of self and a deep belief in angels and the power of prayer. She loved her family, her two grandsons, and her golden retrievers. Lisa Anne was a fighter and despite a near 20-year battle with heart complications, maintained a positivity that was palpable to all she encountered. Her health challenges unfortunately pulled her away from the classroom and kept her adventures closer to home. These limitations never broke her infectious and indomitable spirit and in spite of them, she remained engaged with and even expanded her social community. Lisa Anne had friends far and wide and worked hard to maintain those connections, no matter the distance. Lisa Anne is survived by her beloved husband, Michael Reff, her two daughters, Allison Stalla (Zeid Stalla) and Hayley Swarbrick (Andrew Swarbrick), her two grandsons, Ben Stalla and Grayson Swarbrick, and many friends both near and far. Her life was a testament to the power of perseverance, the joy found in every moment, and the importance of loving deeply and boldly. She would be honored to be forever carried in the hearts of those who knew her. A funeral was held at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland on April 27, 2025, followed by a Continued Celebration of Life at Signature Studios in Roswell, Georgia on May 1, 2025. In lieu of flowers, the family encourages donations to Girls, Inc. of Greater Atlanta (www. girlsincatl.org), where Lisa Anne volunteered for many years.

Rhododendron is a very large genus of about 1,024 species of woody plants. They are found most commonly in acidic and infertile growing conditions and can be either evergreen or deciduous. Most species are native to eastern Asia and the Himalayan region, but smaller numbers occur elsewhere in Asia, and in North America, Europe, and Australia. Their name comes from Ancient Greek with “rhodon” meaning “rose” and “dendron” meaning “tree.” Rhododendrons have no final size and can grow almost indefinitely. They range from dwarf, ground-hugging varieties, which may reach 16 inches, to giant tree-like specimens as tall as 20 feet or more. Most species have brightly colored flowers which bloom from late winter through to early summer. It is the national flower of Nepal, the state flower of both Washington and West Virginia, the state flower of Nagaland, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, and Himachal Pradesh in India, and the provincial flower of Jeju in South Korea and Jiangxi in China. The smaller azalea makes up two subgenera of rhododendron. The large, white, and fuchsia-colored ones on La Salle made a beautiful background for a group photo.
